opening.headline: Learn how to respond to your clients' evidentiary needs by combining security authentication, shared responsibility model, audit log, and compliance API into one picture.
body: Suppose your client's security team asks if you have a SOC 2 report and can produce audit logs of who did what and when. Because our services run on top of external AI providers and in the cloud, some controls are not ours.

In this class, we will look at how to verify authentication in the Trust Center, how to divide the provider and customer's share in a shared responsibility model, the structure of the audit log and Compliance API, and how ABAC and data lineage make access and flow explainable.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the roles of SOC 2, ISO, Trust Center, audit log, and Compliance API
In the shared responsibility model, the responsibilities of the provider and the customer can be separated and analyzed.

screens.lead: Read the two questions in the client's security questionnaire and think about what kind of proof is needed.

visual.alt: A configuration diagram in which two customer questions are scattered and connected to four types of supporting cards: certificate, provider document, audit log, and configuration record.
labels: Can you log who did what and when?

paragraphs: The client's security team sends an inquiry. Is there a SOC 2 report and can you submit audit logs of who did what and when? Since our service runs on an external AI provider and in the cloud, these questions need to be answered partly by the provider and partly by us.

The problem is that the evidence is scattered. The certificate list, the provider's policy document, the log function, and our configuration records are located in different places, making it difficult to know which document is proof of which question.

Also, some controls are not ours. The physical security and infrastructure operation of the data center is the responsibility of the provider. Conversely, we decide what data we put in the prompt and who we give permission to. You can't answer the question accurately if you don't know where responsibility falls.
The questions for this class are: How to organize authentication, responsibility sharing, logs, and access control into one picture.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Can the fact that the provider has a SOC 2 report answer all the questions in the customer questionnaire? At the end of class, think again.

screens.outro: First, let me recall my experience receiving a similar request for proof.

screens.title: Think of a similar situation
screens.lead: If you think about the question yourself first and then make a choice, the summary will unfold. You will not enter or submit an answer. The questions are for thought purposes only.

items.prompt: Has the customer or auditor ever requested documentation or supporting documentation?
items.answer: These requests often come when renewing a contract or bringing in a new client. It takes time to search for documents each time. If you organize in advance what kind of evidence you will provide for each type of question, your response speed will vary.

items.prompt: When a problem occurs while using the cloud, have you ever been confused as to what extent the provider is responsible for?
items.answer: A typical structure is where the provider protects the infrastructure and the customer is responsible for their own data and settings. If we do not know this boundary, we end up putting off responsibility when an accident occurs. It is also important to remember that the boundaries for each service are slightly different.

items.prompt: Have you ever kept track of who used which AI function?
items.answer: Without records, it is impossible to reconstruct what happened when an accident occurred. Audit logs are records that help answer the questions of who, when, what, and where.
It is not recorded. These are thought-provoking questions and will not be submitted or graded.

screens.title: Certification Terminology Basics: SOC 2 Types and ISO Standards
screens.lead: The following flashcards explain six terms you need to know when reading certifications and reports. When you select a card, it flips over and you can move to the next card with the right arrow. Before looking at the certifications in the table, let's first organize what the terms prove.

cards.back: This is a system in which an independent auditor (usually a certified public accountant) evaluates the control of a service organization and submits a report according to the standards set by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA). It is characterized by the fact that it is not a single certificate, but a report containing the auditor's opinion and control explanation.

Evaluates whether controls are appropriately designed at a specific point in time. It tells you whether the design is in place, but it doesn't confirm whether the controls have continued to work over time.

It evaluates not only the design but also the actual operation of the controls over a period of observation. The auditor samples evidence such as access reviews, incident records, and change records during the period. The observation period varies from report to report and often ranges from several months to a year. So, when answering the questionnaire, you must also write down which period the report covers.

These are the five categories that SOC 2 evaluates. Security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy. Security is included by default and the rest is selected by the service organization and included in the report. So the mere presence of a report does not tell us whether availability or even privacy controls have been evaluated.

ISO/IEC 27001 is a standard that sets the requirements for an information security management system (ISMS) and proves whether an organization systematically manages information security risks. ISO/IEC 42001 is a standard that sets the requirements for an AI management system and proves whether an organization that develops, provides, or uses AI has a responsible management system. Both evaluate the organization's management structure, not the performance of the product.

cards.front: Order of reading reports and certificates
cards.back: First, look at the type (whether Type 1 or Type 2) and the target period. Next, we check which trust service criteria categories are included, and finally, whether the products and systems we use are included in the scope of the evaluation. Only when these four things are correct will the questions and evidence in the questionnaire be connected.

screens.outro: Certification is proof of the provider’s infrastructure. So, what is our responsibility? Let’s break it down into a shared responsibility model.

screens.title: Shared Responsibility Model

While reading, choose an AI service that you operate or use, and try to match this to what evidence for that service. This is proof that the point at which the connection is blocked is not yet ready. tabs.label: basic structure
tabs.body:
The shared responsibility model is a structure in which the provider is responsible for cloud security (of), and the customer is responsible for security within the cloud (in). There is a division between safely operating the infrastructure and services themselves and safely using what is installed on them.

Depending on which service is selected, the customer's scope of responsibility for setting up will vary. When renting a virtual server, the customer's share increases, and when using a managed service, the provider's share increases.

tabs.label: Provider's share
tabs.body:
The Provider protects:
- Hardware
- network
- Facilities
- Infrastructure such as regions

Proof in this area is certification and reports such as SOC 2 or ISO. By receiving this certificate, the Customer confirms that the Provider has infrastructure controls in place.

tabs.label: Customer's Share
tabs.body:
Customer is responsible for:
- magnetic data
-Application
- Access rights
- Encryption settings

No matter how well the provider protects its infrastructure, accidents can occur if customers give too much permission or enter sensitive data carelessly. The certificate does not relieve the customer of setup responsibilities.

tabs.label: In AI service
tabs.body:
The structure is the same for AI services. The provider is responsible for safeguarding the model, but the customer is responsible for what data is included in the prompt and who has access to it.

Therefore, when answering a customer questionnaire, we must present the provider's evidence and our settings records separately.

screens.outro: Now that we've drawn the lines of responsibility, let's look at the entries in the audit log, a key piece of evidence proving our part.

screens.title: Audit log entries
screens.lead: Follow the steps in order to see how each line of the audit log is created and how it is read. While reading, choose an AI service that you operate or use, and try to match this to what evidence for that service. This is proof that the point at which the connection is blocked is not yet ready. Since proof is not a document that is created once and finished, but must be updated whenever settings change, it is recommended to set an update cycle and a person in charge.

steps.title: Step 1. Check the default columns
steps.body: The default columns in the audit log are recording time, actor information, event type, event detail, affected entity, IP address, device ID, user agent, and client platform. These columns come together to describe a single line of events.

steps.title: Step 2. Know what an entity is
steps.body: An entity is what an event affects. Examples include accounts, invitations, projects, project documents, conversations, files, and SSO connections. The log only records the identifier, not the title or content of the conversation. This column lets you know what happened to which object.

steps.title: Step 3. Reorganize who, when, what, and where in one line
steps.body: The key is whether these four questions can be reformulated into one line. If you have actor, time, target, IP, and device information, you can review the situation at the time of an accident.

steps.title: Step 4. Check the collection method
steps.body: Collection methods vary depending on the product and setting, and each method has limitations. Claude Enterprise's audit log export has a limit on the period of time it can be viewed, and the download link is only valid for a short period of time. Organizations using customer-managed keys cannot use the export button to import audit events through the Compliance API. OpenAI's Compliance Platform provides immutable, append-only log events for auditing purposes, which also have a fixed retention period. So, if the period to be preserved as evidence is longer than this upper limit, you must continue to download it and store it separately. You should note that how and how much you collect will depend on your organization's setup.

steps.title: Step 5. Remember that the logs themselves are also subject to audit
steps.body: How long logs are retained and who can view them are also subject to audit. If you just accumulate logs and do not manage their retention period and access rights, the logs will become another sensitive data storage.

screens.outro: Now that we've read the structure of the log, let's look at the Compliance API and access control to bring it into the program.

screens.title: Access control and log terminology
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom and organize the six terms. The first three are ways to determine who can access what, and the last three are tools and procedures for collecting, protecting, and finding logs and data.

data.caption: Terminology of access control methods and auditing and protection tools
rows: least privilege
This is the principle of giving only as much authority as is absolutely necessary for work.
This is the basis for narrowing down the administrator role, API key, and query scope. Even if the key is leaked, the damage is reduced.
RBAC (Role Based Access Control)
This is a method of assigning roles to people and granting authority to the roles.

This is simple when there are only a few roles, such as administrator, auditor, and developer. If exceptions are made for conditions such as department, data classification, or region, there is a limit to the number of roles that can continue to increase.
ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control)
This is a method of determining whether to allow or not by comparing the requesting subject, target, requested action, and environment properties with the policy.

Instead of names or roles, rules are written with attributes such as department, data classification, and access location. Even if the number of tables and users increases, the number of policies does not increase significantly, so the larger the size, the more advantageous it is.
SIEM
It is a tool that collects logs from multiple systems in one place, performs correlation analysis, and reports abnormal signs.
This is a destination for viewing audit logs from AI services and logs from other systems.
DLP
A tool that detects or prevents sensitive data from going where it is not allowed.
It is used to check whether the input that employees paste into external AI contains sensitive information.
eDiscovery
The process of finding, preserving, and collecting electronic materials required for litigation or investigations.
It is used when conversation records need to be preserved or retrieved in accordance with legal requirements.
notes: If you understand RBAC first, you can see what ABAC is solving. RBAC groups permissions based on people, and ABAC writes policies based on the attributes of the request. In environments with few roles and simple rules, RBAC is sufficient. The general explanation is that ABAC becomes more advantageous as conditions become more diverse.
NIST's ABAC Guide defines ABAC as a logical access control method that allows access by matching the attributes of subjects, objects, actions, and sometimes environmental conditions against policies.

screens.title: Compliance API and access control
screens.lead: Expand the topic to read what the Compliance API provides and who can use it. While reading, choose an AI service that you operate or use, and try to match this to what evidence for that service. This is proof that the point at which the connection is blocked is not yet ready. Also think about the relationships between entities: how key permissions and network restrictions overlap. The principle of having keys and scopes with least privilege applies here as well.

items.title: What gives you access
items.body: The Claude Compliance API provides programmatic access to activity feeds, lists of users, roles and groups, settings in effect, chat, files and projects, and sessions across multiple products.

items.title: Who writes where?
items.body: Security, legal, and compliance teams use it to audit activity, view or delete content, and integrate with subordinate tools.

items.title: Who makes the keys?
items.body: In Enterprise organizations, only the primary owner can turn the Compliance API on and off. A key can be created to encompass all organizations to which the primary owner is connected, or the owner can create a key that is specific to his or her organization, and the screen is not visible to administrators. Querying the activity feed can be done with a key with the read:compliance_activities scope. The narrower the scope, the less damage there will be if the key is leaked.

items.title: Network and Organizational Limitations
items.body: IP whitelisting only accepts requests from approved IP addresses, while tenant restrictions only allow organizations listed in the headers placed by the network proxy. Both are devices that restrict access paths independently of keys or logins. IP allowlisting is an Enterprise feature, and tenant restrictions are available in Enterprise plans and Console organizations.

items.title: Connections to other tools
items.body: OpenAI's Compliance Platform enables you to connect workspace logs to eDiscovery, DLP, and SIEM tools, and describes two approaches: a log platform for auditing and an API to query the status at the time of the request. Either way, the purpose of collecting, analyzing, and storing logs in one place is the same.

screens.outro: Logs and APIs are proof of activity. Now let's look at access control and flow tracking for the data itself.

states.label: Access Control (ABAC)
states.body:
ABAC is a method of determining whether to allow or not by comparing the properties of the subject, target, requested action, and environment with the policy. In Databricks Unity Catalog, properties expressed as governing tags are written into policy conditions, and policies are attached to the catalog or schema level to apply row filters and column masks consistently across multiple tables. Because rules are written with attributes such as department, data classification, and access location instead of the person's name, it is easy to manage even when the scale grows.

Databricks Unity Catalog displays the same table differently for each user with row filters, column masks, and tag-based ABAC policies. A row filter excludes rows that do not meet the conditions from the query results, and a column mask hides column values.

Google's Security Controls document tabulates support for controls such as Data Residency, CMEK, VPC Service Controls, and Access Transparency. This is the first source to check whether the required controls are supported by the product.

states.label: Data Lineage
states.body:
Data Lineage tracks where data comes from and where it goes. Tables, ML models, and external assets are displayed in a single graph.

There are four reasons why you need Lineage.
- Verify that the data can be trusted.
- Track down the cause when a problem occurs.
- Understand where changes affect you.
- Gain visibility into where sensitive data is being used.

If access control answers who can see it, Lineage answers where this data comes from and where it goes. The two must come together to make data flow explainable.

screens.title: Commentary: Distinguishing between provider and customer responsibilities in the shared responsibility model
screens.lead: Assuming you run a customer service summary service as a cloud AI provider, read through the different areas of responsibility. While reading, choose an AI service that you operate or use, and try to match this to what evidence for that service. This is proof that the point at which the connection is blocked is not yet ready. Since proof is not a document that is created once and finished, but must be updated whenever settings change, it is recommended to set an update cycle and a person in charge.

stops.body: The provider is responsible for maintaining infrastructure security, model service safeguards, and authentication. Since we do not operate this part ourselves, we obtain proof from the provider's documents. Trust Center certification and reports are representative evidence. However, we must check whether the products we use fall within the scope of the certification.

We decide what data we put in the prompt, who we give permission to, and how we set the keys and retention settings. Proof of this area is not in the provider documentation, but rather in our setup records. Even if the provider is safe, accidents can occur if we indiscriminately include the entire consultation content or leave administrator rights wide open.

Activation and storage of logs is a common area where the provider gives the functionality and the customer turns it on and confirms. The fact that a feature exists is different from the fact that it is turned on. We must check and record the settings turned on, storage period, and access rights.

When answering a customer's questionnaire, we divide the evidence into the provider's documents and our settings records. For infrastructure questions, we attach provider documentation, and for permissions and retention questions, we attach our configuration records. If you divide it like this, it will be revealed in the document itself who is responsible.

data.startLabel: Reading from the perspective of evidence

steps.title: Step 1. Prove who has authority to collect
steps.body: The Compliance API is turned on by the primary owner, and scoped keys are created by the primary owner or owner. Administrators will not see this settings screen. This structure provides evidence that collection authority is limited to a few people and that the principle of least privilege is applied.

steps.title: Step 2. Proof what happened with a list of activities
steps.body: The activity feed shows the type, time, and actor of an event. The content of the conversation will not be imported. So this is proof that you can explain who did what and when without opening the content.

steps.title: Step 3. Prove the necessity and records of contents inquiry
steps.body: Retrieve content from chats, files, and projects only when it's absolutely necessary for your investigation. Access to view the content itself is subject to audit, so it must be possible to explain who viewed the content and why. This serves as proof that only the required amount of viewing was carried out.

steps.title: Step 4. Demonstrate long-term storage and analysis system
steps.body: Send imported events to SIEM, DLP, and archiving systems for analysis and long-term storage. Having them all in one place allows you to see correlations with logs from other systems. This is proof that logs are not only accumulated, but are also utilized and preserved.

steps.title: Step 5. Rain testifies to parts and limits.
steps.body: The target range varies depending on the product and plan. Organizations that use customer management keys have different export methods, and a separate Compliance access key with the appropriate scope is required to view content such as chat content or session records. In some cases, your Admin API key will only view your activity feed. Since the scope of collection is the scope of evidence, what is missing must be written down in documentation.

data.text: There is appropriate evidence for each question in the customer inquiry. For the question of independent certification, Trust Center's SOC 2 and ISO Report is provided, along with the scope of applicable products. For the question of handling regulatory data, Trust Center's HIPAA Covered Product Table and Agreement Scope Document is provided. For the question of access logs, the audit log structure and Compliance API collection settings are provided. For the question of data origin, Lineage graph and access control policy is provided. Each piece of evidence aligns with the scope defined by the Write down the time of writing and the product applied. question.

marks.span: Trust Center's SOC 2 and ISO Report
marks.note: This is proof of the provider’s infrastructure control. We check the type of report, the period covered, and whether the product we are writing about is in scope.

marks.span: HIPAA Covered Product Table and Agreement Scope Document
marks.note: Whether or not HIPAA applies is only meaningful if the product and the scope of the contract match. Tables and contract documents are presented together.
Access records are not proven by the fact that there are logs, but by the settings that they are actually collected and stored.

marks.span: Lineage graph and access control policy
marks.note: It shows where the data comes from, how it moves, and who can see it.

marks.span: Write down the time of writing and the product applied.
marks.note: The validity of evidence is tied to its timing and scope. Evidence that does not fit the scope of the question actually leads to misunderstanding.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Let's combine the contents of this lesson into one picture. Answer the reflection questions yourself, but do not record or submit your answers. Among the evidence covered today, choose one thing to check first. The purpose is to organize the answers yourself.

paragraphs: Since the scope of certification varies by product, check applicable products at the Trust Center. The shared responsibility model divides the provider's infrastructure responsibilities and the customer's data, permissions, and configuration responsibilities. Certification is proof of the front and must be proven by our records on the back.

Audit logs allow you to reconstruct who did what and when, and are collected through the Compliance API. ABAC and data lineage make data access and flow explainable. When answering the questionnaire, group these materials by question and write down the timing and scope.

In the end, compliance isn't just about gathering paperwork; it's about maintaining the ability to show what we control at all times. You need to make it a habit to regularly check your settings, logs, and documents to ensure they do not deviate from each other.
If you create a table that organizes the list of evidence by question, you can just update it without looking for it from scratch every time a new customer inquiry comes.

glossary.def: It is a reporting system in which an independent auditor evaluates the control of a service organization. Type 1 evaluates the design at one point in time, and Type 2 evaluates the operational effectiveness over a certain period of time.
A window where providers collect and disclose certifications, reports, and policy documents
How security responsibilities are shared between providers and customers
API that allows programmatic access, auditing, and collection of an organization's activities and content
Records tracking the source and movement/transformation path of data

It is a method of allowing access by comparing the properties of the subject, object, action, and environment, rather than roles, with the policy, and is more advantageous than role-based (RBAC) in environments with diverse conditions.

misconceptions.myth: With certification, our services also comply with regulations.
misconceptions.fact: In the shared responsibility model, customer setup responsibility remains.

misconceptions.myth: Certification applies equally to all products.
misconceptions.fact: The scope varies by product, plan, and hosting path.

misconceptions.myth: Turning on the audit log will take care of itself.
misconceptions.fact: Retention periods, access rights, and collection scope must also be managed.

misconceptions.myth: Anytime there is a SOC 2 report, it means that the controls were operational.
misconceptions.fact: Type 1 evaluates only the design at one point in time, while Type 2 only evaluates operations over a defined observation period. The included trust service criteria categories and evaluation scope also vary from report to report, so you should check the type and target period.
